name: Potato
what: A tuber of the Andes, domesticated around Lake Titicaca 7,000-10,000 years ago. Spanish ships brought it to Europe in the 1560s; it took Europe two centuries to trust it.
why: Nathan Nunn and Nancy Qian estimate the potato explains about a quarter of the growth in Old World population and urbanisation from 1700 to 1900. Relying on one crop also set up the Irish famine of 1845-1852.
now: The world's third most eaten food crop after rice and wheat; China and India grow the most.

sources.cite: Nunn, N. & Qian, N. (2011). The Potato's Contribution to Population and Urbanization. Quarterly Journal of Economics 126(2), 593-650.
Reader, J. (2008). Propitious Esculent: The Potato in World History. Heinemann.

stops.note: Brought to China by Dutch and Spanish ships through Taiwan and the Fujian coast in the 1600s; it spread in the hills where rice would not grow, and boomed in the 1700s.
Portuguese and English ships brought the potato to India's west coast; the traveller John Fryer saw potatoes at Surat in the 1670s. It became a field crop under British rule in the 1800s.

Potato blight (Phytophthora infestans) arrived from the Americas in 1845. About a million people in Ireland died and a million emigrated by 1852; Skibbereen in County Cork became a byword for the famine.
stops.meet: a family in Skibbereen in the winter of 1846
